strengths: Addresses an underexplored but legitimate problem of incorporating visual-interactive capabilities into universal embedding models with clear motivation
Substantial benchmark creation effort (1M samples, 5 datasets, careful human verification and filtering)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 36 MMEB tasks with extensive ablations, hyperparameter studies, and practical case studies
Well-organized presentation with clear methodology description and commitment to reproducibility
Demonstrates practical applications (in-the-wild retrieval, on-the-fly correction with visual hints)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (Qwen2-VL, SAM-2, standard MLPs/contrastive learning) without meaningful algorithmic innovation

Problematic evaluation methodology with circular logic: method designed for visual-interactive tasks, benchmark created for those tasks, with baselines not designed for this capability, making comparisons fundamentally unfair

Critical finding undermining benchmark validity: Table 7 shows that models finetuned on SCaR-train often degrade on MMEB (e.g., VLM2Vec-2B: 58.7→35.8), suggesting potential data quality issues or misalignment with general multimodal understanding

Modest and diminishing improvements: +3.1-8.5% on MMEB-2B, but when baselines are properly finetuned on MMEB-train, improvements collapse to near zero (e.g., VIRTUE-2B vs. Qwen2-VL-2B: 64.1 vs. 63.7 = +0.4)
Inadequate ablation study that conflates multiple factors and fails to isolate the specific contribution of visual prompts through controlled experiments
Unaddressed computational overhead: SAM-2 segmentation at inference adds substantial cost; no analysis of inference time, memory, or efficiency compared to baselines
Limited scope: only bounding boxes and masks explored; no evidence of generalization beyond the specific SCaR task formulation
Reproducibility limited by releasing only 'partial' SCaR benchmark samples due to file size constraints; exact release timeline unspecified

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates the limitation of existing VLMs lacking visual-interactive capabilities, addressing a genuine need in the field
Substantial benchmark contribution: SCaR comprises 1M carefully curated samples from 5 datasets with rigorous construction (GPT-4V generation + human verification + multi-stage filtering)

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: Tests on 36 MMEB datasets plus custom SCaR benchmark, extensive baseline comparisons, thorough ablations, hyperparameter studies, and both in-domain and out-of-domain analysis
Strong experimental results: Consistent 3.1%-8.5% improvements on MMEB tasks and 15.2%-20.3% on SCaR, demonstrating effectiveness across diverse scenarios

Practical and flexible framework: Integrates SAM-2 with segmentation-language connector to handle diverse visual interaction modalities while maintaining competitive performance on standard benchmarks
Good reproducibility: Detailed implementation details in appendices, promised code and benchmark release, comprehensive supplementary materials with clear descriptions of procedures
Excellent presentation: Well-written with informative figures (especially architecture overview), well-organized tables, and clear exposition making the work accessible
Careful dataset construction: Multi-stage pipeline with LLM-based verification, human inspection, and diverse negative generation strategies demonstrates attention to dataset quality
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components are not novel—SAM-2 is existing work, segmentation-language connector is simple (2D conv + MLPs), contrastive learning is standard. Contribution is primarily in engineering and integration rather than methodological innovation
Insufficient computational cost analysis: No discussion of inference time overhead, memory costs of running SAM-2, or practical deployment considerations—important for real-world applicability
Heavy dependence on SAM-2: Visual-interactive capability entirely depends on SAM-2's segmentation quality, but failure modes and error propagation are not thoroughly analyzed

Improvement attribution unclear: SCaR fine-tuning results (Table 7) suggest improvements may partly come from additional training data rather than the method's inherent superiority, confounding the source of gains

Limited scope of visual-interactive evaluation: While SCaR is comprehensive for region-to-text retrieval, evaluation on other visual-interactive tasks (VQA, captioning, referring expressions) would strengthen generality claims
Incomplete failure mode analysis: Qualitative examples are predominantly positive cases; limited discussion of when and why the method fails or performs poorly

Hyperparameter sensitivity not fully characterized: Multiple hyperparameters (τ, LoRA settings, N, |S|) affect performance; unclear how extensively tuned and whether settings generalize across diverse tasks
Limited exploration of interaction modalities: Focuses primarily on bounding boxes and masks; other modalities (scribbles, freeform points) mentioned as supported but not evaluated

SCaR benchmark construction limitations: Reliance on GPT-4V could introduce systematic biases that propagate to the benchmark; construction doesn't introduce fundamentally new benchmark design principles

strengths: Novel problem formulation identifying visual-interactive capabilities as an important but overlooked modality for embedding models
High-quality benchmark construction: SCaR with 1M samples, sophisticated negative generation (3 types), multi-stage filtering, high inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.89), and diverse source datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive ablations (9 dimensions), robustness analysis (jitter/masking/offset), prompt type analysis, and multiple operational mode comparisons
Consistent and substantial improvements on visual-interactive tasks (6.3-20.3% on SCaR), with reasonable gains on MMEB across all meta-tasks
Impressive stability on catastrophic forgetting: VIRTUE maintains MMEB performance when finetuned on SCaR while other baselines show severe degradation (19.8-59 point drops)
Strong reproducibility support: code/models/benchmark to be released, detailed implementation documentation, and clear data collection procedures with prompt templates
Practical demonstrations of real-world applications: visual-interactive I2I retrieval and on-the-fly correction with visual hinting
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core approach straightforwardly combines SAM2 with VLM via simple concatenation; segmentation-language connector is just Conv2D + 2 MLPs (Eq. 1)
Modest improvements on main MMEB benchmark: only +2.0 points for 7B model (66.6→68.6), raising questions about whether added computational complexity is justified for non-interactive scenarios

Concerning dependency on uniform point sampling: removing uniform points drops MMEB by 3.1 points (Table 5), suggesting model becomes dependent on segmentation rather than learning universally better representations

Limited scope of visual-interactive evaluation: SCaR only evaluates image-to-text with bounding boxes; interactive image-to-image retrieval relegated to appendix case studies due to copyright/ethical concerns

Unfair SCaR comparisons: VIRTUE natively handles visual prompts while baselines adapted through text descriptions, making it difficult to isolate benefits; other baselines not originally designed for this task
Computational overhead not well justified: +82ms inference latency (5x slower) and +1.1GB memory with modest MMEB improvements; cost-benefit analysis missing

SCaR quality concerns: 11% sample dropout, synthetic caption generation via GPT-4V for ADE20K, element-swapping negatives may not reflect real challenging cases, and three-element structure somewhat artificial
Missing statistical significance testing: no confidence intervals or significance tests despite claiming consistent improvements across benchmarks
Limited failure analysis: insufficient discussion of when VIRTUE underperforms, which object/scene types benefit most from visual interaction, or scenarios where visual prompts hurt performance

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing underexplored visual prompts for embedding models
Substantial benchmark contribution with 1M samples, careful negative generation, and rigorous quality control (inter-annotator κ=0.89)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablations, robustness analysis, and qualitative results
Practical demonstration of on-the-fly correction and in-the-wild applications
Commitment to reproducibility through promised code/model/benchmark release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward composition of SAM2 + VLM with simple connector (Conv2D + MLPs); no novel architecture or training strategies

Confounded MMEB improvements: cannot distinguish gains from visual prompts vs. capacity increase; Table 5 shows 3.1-point drop without uniform points suggesting capacity matters; 2.0-point improvement for 7B models is modest

Ad-hoc design choice of uniform point sampling for non-interactive tasks lacks clear justification; unclear why SAM2 features conditioned on random points should improve general embedding tasks like classification

SCaR benchmark too narrow: only evaluates object-in-context image-to-text retrieval; image-to-image interactive retrieval relegated to appendix due to 'ethical concerns'; cannot assess full breadth of visual-interactive scenarios

Unfair baseline comparisons: baselines receive text descriptions while VIRTUE gets native visual prompt support; different backbones used (LLaVA-8B vs Qwen2-VL); missing simpler baselines like text region descriptions

Generalization concerns: Table 10 shows SCaR-train finetuning degrades MMEB performance for all baselines (UniME: 66.6→59.0, −7.6 points), indicating distribution shift; VIRTUE more stable but trend present; training only on MMEB+SCaR acknowledged as limiting

Heavy GPT-4V dependence introduces systematic biases; only 11% samples removed after filtering seems low; bounding boxes used instead of masks because GPT-4V 'struggles to interpret them reliably', limiting modality coverage

Missing analysis: no comparison of text descriptions vs. visual prompts; insufficient investigation of when visual prompts help; lacks clear guidance for practitioners; 24% inference overhead (422ms vs 340ms) not adequately discussed
Ablation ambiguities: Phi-3.5-V underperforms despite more parameters (Table 9), suggesting VLM choice confounds results; SAM2.1-L degrades performance vs SAM2.1-B+ (counterintuitive and unexplained)

Core claim incompletely validated: paper claims visual prompts improve universal embeddings, but MMEB improvements could stem from capacity rather than visual prompts; visual prompts primarily validated on narrow SCaR task

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to systematically study visual-interactive capabilities in embedding models, addressing a clear gap in the literature
High-quality benchmark (SCaR): 1M samples with rigorous multi-stage quality control (0.89 Cohen's Kappa), diverse datasets, and challenging element-swapped negatives
Solid technical approach: Intuitive integration of SAM2 with VLMs; design choices (frozen SAM2, uniform points for non-interactive tasks) are well-motivated
Comprehensive evaluation: 36 MMEB + 5 SCaR tasks with extensive ablations, robustness analysis, case studies, and latency/memory analysis
Consistent improvements: 3.1%-8.5% on MMEB, 15.2%-20.3% on SCaR, with strong qualitative results showing practical utility
Strong reproducibility: Detailed implementation, transparent hyperparameters, promised code/model/benchmark release
Opens new research direction: Establishes visual-interactive embeddings as a viable and valuable research area
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing models (VLM + SAM2); segmentation-language connector is standard Conv2D+MLPs; uses off-the-shelf contrastive learning
Dataset construction concerns: Heavy reliance on GPT-4V for generation; ADE20K captions entirely AI-generated without human ground truth; ~11% evaluation samples filtered during quality control
Modest improvements on existing benchmarks: Only 2.0-point gain over UniME-7B on MMEB (68.6 vs. 66.6); most dramatic gains are on newly-introduced SCaR, raising overfitting concerns
Narrow scope of visual-interactive evaluation: SCaR focuses exclusively on I2T with bounding boxes; I2I retrieval only in appendix case studies; no systematic evaluation with points/masks
Computational overhead: 422ms inference per sample (23% slower than text-only); training requires 219 GPU-hours total; may limit practical deployment
Training data limitations: Constrained to MMEB+SCaR only due to computational resources; authors acknowledge more diverse data would improve universality, weakening 'universal' claims

Incomplete analysis: No visualization of learned segmentation features, no failure case analysis, limited discussion of when visual prompts help, no user studies validating practical utility of visual interaction
